title: Trace Facet Journey Mapper — multi-span sequence filters & sticky correlation lanes
creator: Avery Chen
description: Design proposal and interactive prototype for a Trace Facet Journey Mapper inside Redwood Console. Goal: give engineers a fast way to locate, compare, and act on multi-span request sequences across services using correlation lanes, persistent filters, and timeline alignment. This ticket covers layout, interaction model, and acceptance criteria for the first shipping iteration (read-only explorer + export).
acceptance_criteria: Users can filter requests by correlation ID, service, span name, and custom span tags using a persistent facet bar.
Selecting a request opens a compact request card with timeline scrubber, top N spans, and a snapshot of structured tags/metadata.
Multi-select spans across requests to surface aligned timelines and latency bands for quick comparison.
A sticky correlation lane persists pinned correlation IDs at the top of the trace list while users scroll and apply filters.
Prototype flows validated in usability tests with 6 engineers showing median task completion time improvement >25% vs current Console trace list.
Export CSV of selected span rows with timestamp, service, span name, duration, correlation_id, and selected tags works from UI.
Accessibility: keyboard nav for facet selection, spans focus state, and ARIA labels for timeline scrubber.
Performance: initial render of up to 200 trace rows under 600ms on mid-tier hardware (tracked by ENG telemetry).
design_decisions: Use a horizontal 'correlation lane' strip above the trace list so pinned correlation IDs remain visible while scrolling details below.
Faceted filters are additive and support both includes/excludes; applied filters show as chips with a small badge indicating matching count (deferred to runtime telemetry for exact counts).
Timeline alignment: offer 'align by start', 'align by longest span', or 'align by correlation' to support different debugging mental models.
Multi-span selection aggregates durations into latency bands (p95, p99) visually shaded on the timeline for quick hotspots.
Keep the first iteration read-only; mutation actions (tag edit, annotation) will be a follow-up once backend events are supported.
Right-side flyout shows expanded request context; it can be pinned. The flyout reuses existing Console design tokens to reduce dev overhead.
Cost overlay (per-token or per-inference unit) is available as an opt-in layer to correlate expensive requests with trace characteristics; this is read-only and computed server-side.
Avoid full waterfall re-render on every filter change — use client-side diffing to animate in/out trace rows for perceived performance.
tradeoffs: Sticky correlation lanes consume vertical real estate; to balance, we keep lanes compact and collapsible. Some users will prefer larger lanes — that's a later preference setting.
Showing exact match counts for every facet is expensive at scale; we surface approximate counts initially and plan to wire accurate counts via a batched backend endpoint in ENG-3412.
Aggressive timeline alignment provides strong comparison value but can introduce cognitive dissonance when spans have different semantics; alignment modes are explicit to avoid surprises.
First iteration is read-only which limits immediate actionability (annotations/rollouts) but speeds delivery and reduces backend scope.
